topics.title: Cylinder balance (EGT spread)
topics.template: Your engine computer sets the fuel and spark for each cylinder, so the four exhaust gas temperatures (EGTs) should keep a consistent pattern from flight to flight. This topic measures the spread between the hottest and the coolest cylinder in cruise. It compares that spread with your own past flights in similar outside air temperature, and with the Operators Manual limit of {limit:egt_split_high_flow} (which applies when fuel flow is above {profile:egt_spread.high_flow_threshold_lph}). It also watches whether the spread is slowly growing as engine hours build up. A widening spread can point to an injector, spark plug or ignition problem. A single unusual flight is worth noting; a spread that keeps growing over several flights is worth raising with your mechanic. When one cylinder on its own explains the change, it's reported under Cylinder EGT deviation instead, so you see it once.

topics.title: Cylinder EGT deviation
topics.template: Every engine has its own cylinder pattern, and on many one cylinder always runs hotter than the rest. Instead of judging cylinders against a generic ideal, this topic compares each cylinder's cruise EGT, measured against the average of the other three, with that same cylinder's own history. It flags a flight that's clearly outside the cylinder's usual range once there are at least {rule:egt_cyl_deviation.baseline_deviation.n_min} comparable flights, and a steady drift up or down as engine hours build up. A cylinder running hotter than usual can mean a lean injector; one running cooler can point to ignition or a spark plug; erratic readings often point to the EGT probe itself. If the change also means a different cylinder is now the hottest, the message says so.

topics.title: Oil temperature peak
topics.template: This shows the highest oil temperature reached during the flight and compares it with your usual peak on flights in similar outside air temperature. Short flights often end before the engine is fully warm, so a lower peak after a short hop is normal. A peak well above your usual can point to reduced oil cooling, for example less airflow through the oil cooler, a partial blockage, or a long climb on a hot day. A peak well below your usual on a full-length flight can mean the oil isn't getting warm enough. If the oil went past the Operators Manual limit of {limit:oil_temp_max}, that's reported once, under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge.

topics.title: Coolant temperature peak
topics.template: The cylinder heads are liquid-cooled through the radiator, and this shows the highest coolant temperature reached during the flight, compared with your usual peak on flights in similar outside air temperature. Short flights often end before the engine is fully warm, so a lower peak after a short hop is normal. A peak well above your usual can point to the cooling system: airflow through the radiator, coolant level, the pressure cap or the thermostat. A peak well below your usual on a full-length flight is less common and worth a look at the sensor. If the coolant went past the Operators Manual limit of {limit:coolant_temp_max}, that's reported once, under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge.

topics.title: Time at takeoff power
topics.template: The Operators Manual allows takeoff power, above {profile:overboost.rpm_threshold} or {profile:overboost.power_pct_threshold} power, for no more than {profile:overboost.limit_s} at a time. This topic measures the longest continuous stretch you spent there on this flight. Going past the limit is reported under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge. Coming within {profile:overboost.close_call_margin_s} of it is noted as a close call: it often means power wasn't reduced promptly after takeoff, for example during a long climb-out or a delay. Reducing to climb power once you're safely airborne keeps you well clear.
topics.text: The Operators Manual allows takeoff power, above 5500 rpm or 100% power, for no more than 300 s at a time. This topic measures the longest continuous stretch you spent there on this flight. Going past the limit is reported under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge. Coming within 60 s of it is noted as a close call: it often means power wasn't reduced promptly after takeoff, for example during a long climb-out or a delay. Reducing to climb power once you're safely airborne keeps you well clear.

topics.title: Turbo boost at takeoff
topics.template: At full takeoff power the turbocharger should deliver a manifold pressure (MAP) that depends mainly on airport elevation and outside air temperature. This topic learns that relationship from your own takeoffs and compares each takeoff's MAP with what your engine normally makes in the same conditions. A takeoff is flagged when the difference is larger than your takeoffs normally vary, about {config:outlier_z_threshold} times the usual scatter of your own data. Lower than expected can point to the turbo, the wastegate or an intake leak; higher than expected is usually worth a sensor check. If a takeoff's elevation or temperature is outside anything your takeoffs have covered so far, the card says so instead of guessing.

topics.title: Engine computer alerts in flight
topics.template: The ENGINE ECU caution comes from the engine computer, and when it appears matters more than that it appears. This topic sorts each occurrence by the flight phase it happens in. At start, while the avionics and the engine computer come up, during the lane check, when each lane is tested on its own, and at shutdown, it is expected and is not flagged. An occurrence on the ground with the engine running, while taxiing or idling, is listed as a ground event but is not flagged here either. Only an occurrence in flight, from the takeoff roll to the landing roll, is flagged; it is not expected, and it is worth having the engine computer's fault log read at the next maintenance. Occurrences shorter than {profile:cas.min_event_duration_s} are counted separately and not treated as events, since a single reading can be a logging artefact.

topics.title: Operators Manual limits
topics.template: This checks every reading the engine reports against the limits in the Rotax Operators Manual for your engine: temperatures, pressures, RPM, manifold pressure, voltage, EGT split and time at takeoff power. Moments when a reading is expected to be out of range, such as engine start, warm-up or the fuel pump test, are allowed for, and very brief blips are ignored. Each limit that was exceeded appears once, with how long and by how much, and links to that moment on the chart. If a limit is exceeded on every flight because of a known sensor or installation characteristic, you can set a filter with a note; the app keeps watching the filtered limit and tells you if the pattern changes.

topics.title: Flight summary numbers
topics.template: Fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon and average cruise fuel flow are shown for planning, not as engine-health checks. They mostly reflect wind, weight and the power setting you chose rather than the engine itself: miles per gallon uses ground speed, so a headwind lowers it, and fuel flow is an estimate calculated by the engine computer, not a measurement. That's why these numbers never raise an alert.
